title: What comes from adf-hx, what is ours

slides.title: What comes from adf-hx, and what is ours
slides.lede: Every number in this deck was read out of the repository, not estimated.

slides.title: Six upstream packages, 26 MB installed
slides.lede: Three are Alfresco's, one is Hyland's client, and one — `adf-hx-content-services` — is available **only** from GitHub Packages, which is why the whole `@alfresco` scope is pointed there.
slides.footnote: Tarball sizes were measured by downloading each one during Phase 0 and re-confirmed in Phase 2. `hxcs-js-client` is shown at its version rather than a measured size.

slides.title: Five upstream components. Thirteen of ours.
slides.lede: The `Hxp*` prefix is upstream's naming convention, and our bridge components mirror it — so the prefix tells you nothing about origin. What tells you is the import.
slides.footnote: Phase 3 reported "8 of 8 components delivered". Search is **ours**, not adopted: our component consuming upstream's list. Permissions started as a read-only display of ours and is now upstream's own panel. Upstream's Properties and Versions sidebars left this route in NXSAT-290, so its folder tabs match production browse; both panels stay on the document page.

slides.title: Twelve API ports, and one rule
slides.lede: Upstream talks to a Hyland content service. We talk to Nuxeo. The bridge implements upstream's twelve API tokens against Nuxeo's REST API — and keeps adf-hx types out of our public surface entirely.

items.label: API ports bound
items.sub: DOCUMENT, QUERY, MODEL, UPLOAD, DOWNLOAD, VERSION, CHECKIN, COPY, MOVE, RENDITIONS, USER, GROUP

items.label: adf-hx types in our public API
items.sub: Enforced by `checkNoAdfHxInPublicApi()`, a gate that has been watched failing

slides.footnote: The rule matters because a leaked upstream type would make every customer of `@nuxeo/satori-platform` depend on adf-hx, and pull `adf-core` into their bundle whether they use it or not.

slides.title: Adoption is not free, and the price is written down
slides.lede: Every workaround, gap, refusal and degradation has an ID, a register row, and a marker in the source. A gate fails if a marker exists without a row, or a row without a marker.
slides.footnote: 29 rows recorded in `docs/adf-hx-workarounds.md`, of which **20 markers are still live** in the source — 12W/7M/6D/4R recorded, 6W/5M/5D/4R live, so 9 have been closed. A gate fails if a marker exists without a row, or a row claims a marker no source file carries.

slides.title: The bridge is the small part
slides.lede: Adopting upstream components did not shrink our codebase — it moved effort into the adapter and left the product surface ours.

items.note: browse, search, document detail, admin, tasks…

items.note: the whole cost of speaking upstream's protocol

slides.footnote: Lines of TypeScript, excluding specs. The bridge is 10% of the code and carries most of the integration risk — which is why it is the layer with its own architecture document.

slides.title: adf-core is eager, and that is a real 1.15 MB
slides.lede: Eleven upstream services are `providedIn: 'root'` and resolve the port tokens from the root injector. Providing the ports on a component instead fails one `NG0201` at a time — that was tried.
slides.footnote: Initial bundle, production configuration. The forkable template imports only `/extensions` and `/app-config`, which is why it is 9× smaller than the product.

slides.title: Upstream gives us the document surface. We give it Nuxeo.

blocks.text: Seven components come from adf-hx. Twelve API ports, thirteen bridge components and the entire four-layer extensibility contract are ours — and that contract is what a customer actually programs against.
